newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn appears closer to Telekom share sale.
newsitem.headline: Bonn appears closer to Telekom share sale.

text.p: The German government on Tuesday appeared to move ahead with a plan to cash in Deutsche Telekom AG shares to help cut its debt mountain, although the exact timing and mechanics of the move remained unclear.

Government sources on Tuesday said Bonn was considering selling 287 million shares this year and the remainder by the end of 1998, and Telekom confirmed the company was holding talks with the finance ministry.

"We will certainly sell our shares faster than had hitherto been planned," Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch told German news channel n-tv according to extracts from an interview to be aired later in the day.
Boetsch added that how state-owned shares in the German telephone monopoly would be sold had not yet been decided, but he was looking at three options:
-- A bourse flotation, which would not require legislation.
-- The sale of shares to a strategic partner.
-- The disposal of the state's entire stake.
Telekom spokesman Ulrich Lissek said the company would not keep its right to increase capital, even if Bonn sells its shares. Telekcom wouldn't lose sight of shareholder interests, he told Reuters.
He declined to specify what Telekom and the finance ministry were discussing.
Analysts remained cautious but said a sale of some of Bonn's 2.03 billion shares in Telekom was likely.

"It is difficult and still speculative to suggest exactly what is likely to happen, yet it is clear that Bonn wants to mobilise these funds...sooner rather than later," said one financial analyst in London who did not want to be identified.
In afternoon electronic trading, Telekom shares slid 3.3 percent, or 1.33 marks, to 38.72 marks, going against the blue-chip DAX index, which was up 0.4 percent at 3,674.50.

At the current share price, Bonn could reap a gain of about 11 million marks from selling a packet of 287 million shares. It needed the money to help bring its deficit within the range required for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Referring to Germany's difficulties in qualifying for EMU, Boetsch said the privatisation would take place in such a timely way that "the problems we are now facing can be dealt with satisfactorily".
That meant Finance Minister Theo Waigel should be able to book the proceeds of a further Telekom sale during the current year. "It must be realisable," Boetsch said.
Bonn still controls nearly three-quarters of Telekom after last November's privatisation of a 26 percent stake, which raised 20 billion marks.
A packet of 287 million shares could be parked with a bank and later sold to a strategic partner of Telekom, coalition sources told Reuters.
The shares would then be sold on the market by 2000 at the earliest, they said.
A sale of Telekom shares emerged as a possible measure after estimates showed Bonn would have a 1997 tax revenue shortfall of about nine billion marks.
Boetsch repudiated charges that Bonn was simply raiding its own assets to make the grade for Europe's single currency.
"Nothing is being plundered," he told n-tv. "We are also not selling under pressure. This is not some kind of carpet trading where prices can be dictated."
